sections.h2: Where is Lafayette County, Missouri, and how did it form?
sections.html:
Lafayette County lies in western Missouri on the eastern edge of the Kansas City metro area, and Lexington is the county seat. Wikipedia gives a total area of 639 square miles, of which 628 is land, with Jackson, Ray, Carroll, Saline, Pettis and Johnson counties around it.

The county was organized on November 16, 1820 from Cooper County and first named Lillard County. The legislature renamed it for the Marquis de La Fayette on February 16, 1825, while he was touring the United States. German settlers who arrived around the Civil War shaped towns such as Concordia, Higginsville, Wellington and Napoleon.

The 2020 census counted 32,984 residents, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 33,531. Selling a house in a county this size usually means a short drive to the courthouse square in Lexington for any paperwork.

sections.h2: Which towns and school districts serve Lafayette County?
sections.html:
Lexington, Higginsville, Odessa, Concordia, Wellington, Waverly, Alma and Oak Grove (partly) are among the places in the county, along with smaller towns such as Napoleon, Corder, Dover, Mayview and Bates City. Six public school districts reach into the county, and the one that serves your address shows up as a line on your tax bill.

  • Lexington R-V, with Lexington High School
  • Lafayette County C-1, based in Higginsville
  • Odessa R-VII
  • Concordia R-II
  • Santa Fe R-X, based in Alma
  • Wellington-Napoleon R-IX

Metropolitan Community College counts these districts inside its service area, although the county sits outside its in-district tax area. That detail matters if you compare Lafayette County bills with bills across the Jackson County line, where levies differ.

sections.h2: How does Lafayette County housing compare in the Census data?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau lists the median owner-occupied home in Lafayette County at $216,500 for 2020 to 2024, and 75.7% of households own their homes. Median household income is $80,612 in 2024 dollars, and 9.7% of residents live in poverty.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Lafayette County?
sections.html:
The Assessor values property and the Collector bills and collects it. Craig Williams is the Assessor, located in the Lafayette County Courthouse at 1001 Main Street, Lexington, reachable at (660) 259-6158 or assessor@lafayettecountymo.gov, with office hours from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM on weekdays.

Lori Fiegenbaum has held the Collector's office since March 1, 2003. The Collector of Revenue gathers current and delinquent real and personal property tax for the county and for every taxing district with an authorized levy, then distributes the funds to schools, the library, fire districts and other entities each month.

The Assessor's site offers a public GIS map, and an enhanced version is available by annual subscription. Personal property declarations can be filed online, and the online window closes every May 1.

sections.h2: When are Lafayette County tax bills due, and how do I pay?
sections.html:
Statements go out in early November, are due on receipt, and turn delinquent after December 31. The Collector asks anyone who has not received a statement by Thanksgiving to call (660) 259-6171.

Payments have to carry a postmark no later than December 31. A payment postmarked later comes back unprocessed unless it includes the late fees. All statements can be paid with one check, and the office cannot accept partial or incorrect payments.

  • Online through the Collector's website
  • By mail to P.O. Box 365, Lexington, MO 64067
  • By phone using the 800 number and PIN printed on the statement
  • In the office at 1001 Main Street with cash, personal check, credit card or money order

The Collector's office is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 to 4:30 and stays open at noon. Holiday closings are posted on the collector's home page, so check them before you drive in around Christmas and New Year's.

sections.h2: What senior tax credit does Lafayette County offer?
sections.html:
Lafayette County runs a senior property tax credit under Senate Bill 190 and Senate Bill 756 and section 137.1050 of the Missouri statutes. The commissioners adopted it on April 2, 2025 as Ordinance #25-01, and it applies to a senior's primary residence.

The county's collector page says the 2026 application period is closed and that the site will be updated when the 2027 period opens. Anyone who applied and qualified the previous year does not have to send a renewal. New applicants use the application form posted on the collector's page, and a separate FAQ explains renewals.

If you plan to sell a home that carries this credit, tell the Collector's office so your account is updated, and read the FAQ to see how a change of residence affects the credit.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Lafayette County assessment?
sections.html:
Talk to the Assessor first, then take an appeal to the county Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July. If the Board's answer leaves you unhappy, the State Tax Commission accepts an appeal within 30 days of the date on the Board's letter.

The State Tax Commission also explains how to pay under protest. You pay the full bill to the collector by December 31, write "paid under protest" on the check, and file a written statement that gives your reasons and your own view of the fair market value. If you bought the home less than 30 days after the county mailed the statement, or the assessor never told the owner about a higher value, a direct State Tax Commission appeal is allowed.

Appeals for property held by an LLC, trust, estate, corporation or limited partnership must come from an attorney.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Lafayette County property tax?
sections.html:
The Collector conducts a delinquent tax sale each August. Real estate with taxes unpaid after the December 31 deadline can end up in that sale, so a balance that sat through the spring needs attention before summer.

Missouri's tax sale rules sit in Chapter 140 of the state statutes, and the sale buyer receives a certificate of purchase and not an immediate deed. Ask the Collector for the current sale date, the list and the redemption amounts, because the county's own pages give only the month. A sale of the house while taxes are still open usually means the balance is paid at closing from your proceeds.

Lexington's Recorder of Deeds, also in the courthouse, records the deed after closing, and the Assessor's real estate transfer work follows from that recording.

sections.h2: What should I check before selling a Lafayette County house with tax due?
sections.html:
Get a current statement from the Collector, ask for the payoff in writing, and confirm that both real estate and personal property accounts are clear. The Collector will not take partial payment on a statement, so the payoff has to cover the whole amount.

  • Look at the assessed parcel on the Assessor's GIS map for the correct acreage and address.
  • Check whether a senior credit or other relief applies and how a sale changes it.
  • Ask your title company to prorate the current year in the contract.
  • Keep the paid receipt, since the collector's site lets you print one.

A cash sale does not change what is owed, since the tax follows the parcel. It does shorten the time you carry the bill after you decide to sell.

faqs.q: When are Lafayette County property taxes due?
faqs.a: They are due on receipt and turn delinquent after December 31. Your payment must be postmarked no later than December 31 to avoid penalties.

faqs.q: How do I contact the Lafayette County Collector?
faqs.a: Call (660) 259-6171 on weekdays between 8:30 and 4:30, or write to P.O. Box 365, Lexington, MO 64067. The office is at 1001 Main Street in Lexington.

faqs.q: Who is the Lafayette County Assessor?
faqs.a: Craig Williams is the Assessor. The office is at 1001 Main Street in Lexington, and the phone number is (660) 259-6158.

faqs.q: Can I make a partial tax payment in Lafayette County?
faqs.a: No. The Collector does not accept partial or incorrect payments, though one check may cover all of your statements.

faqs.q: Does Lafayette County have a senior property tax credit?
faqs.a: Yes. Ordinance #25-01 created a credit under Senate Bill 190 for a senior's primary residence. The 2026 application window has closed, and the county will post the 2027 window on the collector's page.
